S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving a battery, including overheating whether or not it results in fire, injury, emergency-service response, or material property damage, to the relevant regulator within 5 calendar days after learning of it, and notify affected customers within 10 calendar days. A fatality or incident presenting an imminent risk to other units must be reported to the regulator within 24 hours, with an initial customer safety notice within 48 hours where a hazard may remain.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before sale and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative samples. Before purchase, each prospective customer must receive the model’s numerical 55 °C failure rate directly and privately, together with clear information about material hazards, safe operating instructions, and any regulator-required precautions. Individual per-model failure rates must not be published or otherwise disclosed to the general public. A failure rate above 5% requires prompt regulator notification, a corrective-action plan, and follow-up testing. Exceeding 5% is not by itself an automatic prohibition on sale or service; the regulator shall determine proportionate additional measures based on the evidence, corrective actions, and risk to users and the public.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: New units manufactured 24 months after this standard takes effect must support secure remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and clear customer instructions. For units already installed on the effective date, manufacturers must offer a compatible retrofit or replacement pathway and complete the program within 6 years, prioritizing higher-risk units.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: New units manufactured 36 months after this standard takes effect must include built-in fire suppression suitable for the unit’s battery chemistry and installation environment. Manufacturers must validate the suppression system and provide installation, inspection, and maintenance instructions to customers. The regulator may approve an equivalent protective design where it provides comparable fire-risk reduction.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: When a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any 12-month period, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers and submit the model for an independent risk review. The regulator must require a recall, including stopping sale and providing repair, replacement, or refund, when the review finds that a recall is necessary to protect users or the public; otherwise it must order proportionate corrective action and follow-up, with its decision and rationale made public.

document.section_notes: The final rules are a compromise that respects both companies' red lines: per-model numerical test results are given privately to customers and regulators but not published publicly; remote shut-off retrofit is required within 6 years; fire suppression is required within 36 months. S1 requires comprehensive incident reporting, while S2 and S5 use regulatory review and corrective-action plans instead of automatic bans/recalls for exceeding thresholds. S3 and S4 set deadlines within the acceptable ranges but not the safest.
